Tonight's Blossom word

RAPATEACEAE

/rəˌpætiˈeɪsiː/  ·  ruh-PAT-ee-AY-see-ee  ·  noun · botanical Latin: a family of flowering plants

The Definition, Translated

Rapateaceae — the rapatea family: a family of monocot flowering plants in the order Poales, almost entirely of tropical South America.

Some 17 genera and 94 species of perennial herbs, nearly all of them growing where almost nothing else will: the bleached white sands and sheer tepui summits of the Guayana Shield — Venezuela, Guyana, Brazil, Colombia. Each plant is a ground-hugging rosette of stiff, sword-shaped leaves, and out of the rosette rises a stalk topped with a compact head of small flowers, often wrapped in bright yellow, orange, or red bracts like a lantern. They are kin to the bromeliads and the cattails, off in their own family in the order Poales — and the family takes its name from its first-described genus, Rapatea, catalogued in French Guiana in 1775.

Say it right: ruh-PAT-ee-AY-see-ee — every plant family in -aceae is said AY-see-ee at the tail. Eleven letters, and seven of them are vowels: A four times, E three. The consonants just hold the trellis up.

"A family that grows where almost nothing else will — on starving white sand and bare stone, at the top of the Lost World." — the rapateads' home ground: the tepui country of the Guayana Shield

Anatomy of the Word

Eleven letters, three working parts — tap each part:

Spelling warning: one P, one C, and the vowels do the heavy lifting — A-P-A, then E-A, then E-A-E. Drop one and Blossom will not pay out.

What It Is

One family, three claims on your attention:

I. The Plant

Perennial herbs with stiff, sword-shaped leaves in ground-hugging rosettes, and compact heads of small flowers — often in bright yellow, orange, or red bracts — held up on stalks like lanterns.

II. The Range

Tropical South America, centered on the ancient Guayana Shield: the white-sand savannas and tepui summits of Venezuela, Guyana, Brazil, and Colombia — some of the poorest soil on Earth, and some of its richest botany.

III. The Outlier

One genus, Maschalocephalus, grows an ocean away in West Africa. Botanists read it as a Gondwanan fingerprint: the family's ancestors were already in place before the Atlantic finished opening.

A Short History of the Family

1775 — Aublet in French Guiana

Jean Baptiste Christophore Fusée Aublet, cataloguing the plants of French Guiana, describes Rapatea paludosa from the swamps — the genus that gives the whole family its name when botanists later promote it to family rank.

Tepui Country — The Lost World Highlands

Most rapateads live up on the tepuis — the sheer-walled table mountains of the Guayana Shield, Conan Doyle's Lost World — or on the bleached white sands below them: ground so poor in nutrients that a whole family's career becomes a study in making do.

Across the Atlantic — One Genus in Africa

Maschalocephalus turns up in the rainforests of Liberia and its neighbors — the family's only African. Either its ancestors were in place before the continents split, or its seeds made a crossing nobody has explained. Either way, it is a long way from the tepuis.

Tonight — Seven Vowels in Eleven Letters

Kip usually passes on the science words. This one he picked — eleven letters, seven of them vowels, and a whole Lost World folded inside it. On tonight's Blossom board, the tepui family flowered.
